analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card late fees at $8 for large card issuers.
analysis.headline: The Credit Card Fairness Act, introduced January 15, 2026, would cap late fees at $8 for large card issuers, but it has sat in the Senate Banking Committee with no action or vote since the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes into federal law a rule the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau issued that limits credit card late fees to $8, and bars large issuers from charging more than it actually costs them when a customer pays late. It applies only to big issuers with 1 million or more open accounts, and the cap can rise only with inflation. Codifying the rule in a statute would protect it from the kind of court challenge that rules made by agencies can face.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card customers who pay late — often people juggling bills or hit by an unexpected expense — would pay at most $8 per late fee instead of the much higher fees large issuers currently charge, which are commonly $30 or more per incident. Because fees are also barred from exceeding the issuer's actual cost, late payers would stop subsidizing issuer profits through penalties. The cap covers issuers with 1 million or more open accounts, which is where most cardholders' accounts sit.

how_it_helps.text: Caps late fees at $8 for any credit card issuer with 1 million or more open accounts, covering the large banks and card companies most cardholders use.
Bars fees above the issuer's actual cost of a late payment, so late fees can no longer contribute to issuer profits — a change from current law, which lets fees exceed costs.
Allows the cap to rise only by the rate of inflation (the Consumer Price Index), so issuers cannot lobby their way to bigger penalties each year.

Requires the CFPB to publicly release the research behind any rule it writes under this provision before the comment period, and channels any court challenge to the D.C. federal district court, replacing the current regime with a statutory cap that is harder to strike down than an agency rule.

analysis.who_pays: Large credit card issuers — the big banks and card companies with 1 million or more accounts — would lose late-fee revenue they currently collect, which under the CFPB's analysis ran into the billions of dollars per year. They could recover some of that through interest rates or other charges. Smaller issuers, including community banks and credit unions under the 1 million-account threshold, are exempt and keep their current fee practices.

drawbacks.text: The cap only applies to issuers with 1 million or more open accounts. Smaller banks and credit unions can still charge uncapped late fees, and an issuer just under the threshold faces a sharp cliff if it grows past it — creating a two-tier market where the same late payment is penalized differently depending on who holds the card.

Issuers argue that when late-fee income is cut, they make up losses through higher interest rates or annual fees, spreading the cost to all cardholders rather than only to those who pay late. This was the core industry objection to the CFPB rule the bill codifies, and a genuinely possible side effect even if the fee savings to late payers are real.

The $8 figure is fixed by statute and can only be adjusted upward by inflation, so if issuers' actual costs of handling late payments change substantially, the cap would not track them — the bill trades precision for a hard, predictable ceiling.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is concrete and falls on the people least able to afford it: a late payment currently can trigger a $30-plus fee, charged repeatedly on a cycle, and this bill cuts that to $8 and removes profit from the penalty. The costs are real but diffuse — issuers may nudge rates or fees upward for everyone, and small issuers are carved out entirely. On balance this is a straightforward consumer protection whose design tradeoffs (the size exemption, the inflation-only adjustment) are reasonable limits, not flaws that undermine the purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2026 and sent straight to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has sat ever since without a hearing, a markup, or a vote — and since Congress is still in session, it could theoretically still move.

narrative.text: Senator John Fetterman introduced the bill on January 15, 2026, joined by Senators Booker and Baldwin as the original cosponsors.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — the standard first stop, where the committee decides whether the bill is worth advancing.

The bill's stated purpose is to codify the CFPB's late fee rule under Regulation Z, locking an $8 cap and a cost-based limit into the Truth in Lending Act itself rather than leaving it as a regulation agencies can revisit or courts can unwind.
As of the latest action record, nothing has happened after the referral — no committee vote, no floor action, and no companion push in the House appears in the bill's history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large credit card issuers are better off so far: as long as the bill sits in committee, they keep collecting late fees above $8 that can exceed their actual costs, and the rule the bill would write into law remains unwritten into law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large credit card issuers, so far

for.name: Sen. John Fetterman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Card Fairness Act on January 15, 2026.

for.name: Sens. Cory Booker and Tammy Baldwin
for.role: Original cosponsors, joined the bill at introduction
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced; five Democratic senators cosponsored in total.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controls whether the bill advances
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 15, 2026 and has taken no action on it since — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history.

against.name: Credit card industry and bank trade groups
against.role: Industry opponents of the underlying late fee cap
against.what_they_did: Fought the CFPB late fee rule in court and in Washington; the rule the bill would codify was challenged and ultimately blocked, which is why a statutory fix was proposed.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, no Republican has signed on, and no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape is suggestive but untested.

industries.industry: Large credit card issuers (big banks and card companies)
industries.note: Issuers with 1 million or more accounts would see late fees capped at $8 and barred from exceeding their actual costs — late fees have historically been a multibillion-dollar, high-margin revenue line for these companies. Their interest in keeping fees above cost runs directly against late-paying customers.

industries.industry: Community banks and credit unions under the account threshold
industries.note: Issuers with fewer than 1 million open accounts are exempt, so they keep charging uncapped late fees while their large competitors are restricted — a relative competitive advantage, though their customers get no new protection.
The bill converts the CFPB's late fee rule into statute, entrenching the agency's framework in law and making the cap far harder for a future administration or court to erase.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in the Senate Banking Committee with a handful of same-party cosponsors and no committee action after referral almost never reach the floor in the same Congress. With Republicans holding the Senate majority and no bipartisan cosponsor on board, the realistic path is that the bill dies quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless sponsors attach it to a larger, must-pass vehicle or it gains major bipartisan support, neither of which shows in the record.
